title: Signs Someone Likes You: What the Research Actually Found
description:
You walk away from a conversation replaying one sentence, certain it went badly. The other person walked away too - and nobody ever checks what they thought.

Somebody checked. Five studies, published in Psychological Science in 2018, same answer every time: people are liked more than they think they are. Talking longer does not close the gap. Self-esteem and narcissism do not predict it. A $100 bonus for guessing accurately moved nothing.

Every figure here is read from the paper itself, with the sample sizes said out loud.

title: Why do we cry?
description:
Crying feels like a release valve. In a diary study of 1,004 crying episodes, only about 30% were followed by feeling better - and in the lab, people who cried at a sad film felt worse straight afterwards. What did predict feeling better was having one person there. Tears are a signal, not a valve.

Source: Gracanin, Bylsma & Vingerhoets (2014), Frontiers in Psychology, 5, 502.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4035568

Describes what was measured. Not advice.

title: Does shouting make the anger smaller?
description:
600 people were made angry, then split three ways: hit a punching bag thinking about the person who angered them, hit it thinking about fitness, or sit quietly for two minutes. The quiet group came out the least angry and the least aggressive. Venting at the thing rehearses it.

Source: Bushman (2002), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 28(6), 724-731.
https://public.websites.umich.edu/~bbushman/PSPB02.pdf

Describes what was measured. Not advice.

title: They raised a chimp as their son's twin
description:
In 1931 a psychologist brought home a baby chimpanzee and raised her alongside his ten-month-old son. Same cot, same food, same rules, for nine months. The question was whether an ape could be raised human. At about a year old the chimp was ahead - and the boy started copying her sounds. They ended it in March 1932 and never explained why.

Source: Kellogg & Kellogg (1933), The Ape and the Child. The Kelloggs left the reason unstated.
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/guy-simultaneously-raised-chimp-and-baby-see-what-would-happen-180952171/

title: They liked you more than you thought
description:
A hundred people at a workshop were asked how interesting they found their partner, and how interesting they thought they were to them. Before talking the gap was 0.37. After talking it was 0.68. Talking to someone made them worse at reading them, not better.

Source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018), Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742-1756.
https://repository.essex.ac.uk/23025/1/The%20Liking%20Gap%20in%20Conversations.pdf
